title: Ex-CIA officer on UK investigations into alleged Iran, Russia threats
description: NPR's Michel Martin speaks with former CIA senior executive clandestine service officer Daniel Hoffman about investigations in Britain into all
body:
NPR's Michel Martin speaks with former CIA senior executive clandestine service officer Daniel Hoffman about investigations in Britain into alleged threats linked to Iran and Russia.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  We wanted to talk these stories over with someone with experience in intelligence gathering. So we've called Daniel Hoffman. He's a former CIA senior executive clandestine service officer. He's now an advisory board member at the global consulting firm, BGR Group. Good morning, Mr. Hoffman.DANIEL HOFFMAN: Good morning.MARTIN: So let's just talk these through separately. In the case of the charges linked to Iran, we just heard about these alleged operatives carrying out attacks remotely, ranging from this FaceTime call from Iran to coded messages, passed from a New York jail. Is there something that strikes you about these details?HOFFMAN: It does. Look, I think many would like to say that the war - U.S. war against Iran is over, but I would argue that in spite of their depleted military, the Iranians still have the capability to inflict harm on the United States. And for sure, our military bases and other critical locations are in the crosshairs for the Iranians. They want to demonstrate that they have the power to target us kinetically, and I think they believe that would give them leverage in whatever negotiations may or may not take place.MARTIN: You know, the DOJ released a detailed narrative about the accused, including photos of them allegedly planning and directing terrorist attacks. How would they get that information?HOFFMAN: Right. Well, a lot of the information that the terrorists would gain would be through open source. These days, what terrorists like to do is conduct surveillance of targets before they strike. And you can do a lot of that with Google Earth and other tools available on the internet. Now, that's also going to give us an opportunity, if we're watching them, to determine or to learn where they might be planning their next attack.MARTIN: So does that suggest to you that these people were under surveillance at the time, but, oh, some of these attacks did take place? I guess that's one of the things that's sort of confusing about this.HOFFMAN: Right, and there are probably ongoing attacks. So when we make arrests like these, and we hold alleged conspirators in custody, we're also at the same time, in an incident response phase, that there are possible attacks that have been attempted and we need to be aware of that. And we need to conduct sort of a damage assessment to understand where other threats may be out there, and then appropriately defend ourselves. We've seen that already at the U.S. Army bases in the U.K., and Iran has targeted our bases in the Middle East as well. They want to degrade the U.S. ability to project power both in the Middle East and globally.MARTIN: Well, I guess what seems so concerning about this is that these threats seem so dispersed. So the question is, you can't surveil everyone. I guess...HOFFMAN: Right.MARTIN: ...That's the - that is the thing that seems so worrying about this. But these groups seem to operate in these small groups or small cells or individually, all over the world at this point. And I'm just wondering, how does one counter something like that?HOFFMAN: Right. So that's definitely the challenge. These groups are operating reportedly at the behest of Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps. So the goal for the United States has always been to recruit sources inside the institutions of our adversaries, whether it's the KGB during the Cold War, or today in Iran, and that way, we may learn something about their planning. But you're absolutely right - when the attacks are being planned in such a dispersed way, without central control, it makes it extraordinarily difficult for us to detect the threat, way out what we like to call left of boom before any harm is caused to our installations or our homeland and then preempt the threat.MARTIN: OK. Before we let you go, we have a minute left here. Let me talk about that other case, the case of the U.S. soldier arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. I do have to emphasize here, no charges have been filed. A lot we don't know. But what questions do you have about this? What's open in your mind about this?HOFFMAN: Well, look, it's quite significant if he was arrested and on suspicion of espionage, that is assisting a foreign intelligence service, obtaining, disclosing protected information. That's a big deal. We don't know when the Russians have recruited him. We don't know what information he passed. To connect these stories together, I can tell you that Russia and Iran have a very robust intelligence-sharing relationship. And so whatever Russia obtained from this U.S. Army officer, quite possibly, most likely, they passed it to the Iranians, not to mention their other allies. China, for example.MARTIN: OK. I'll just say one more time that individuals are innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. I just think it's important to sort of emphasize that since we do not know. That is former CIA senior executive clandestine service officer Daniel Hoffman. He's now with BGR Group. Mr. Hoffman, thanks so much.HOFFMAN: Thank you.

title: Kennedy relatives join the fight against Trump's arch, alleging harm to JFK's grave
description: The gravesite of former President John F
body:
The gravesite of former President John F. Kennedy at Arlington National Cemetery sits on the same axis as the Lincoln Memorial (seen in the distance). Kennedy's relatives say Trump's 250-foot arch would not only disrupt the view between the monuments, but cast a shadow over his grave.
                
                    Jewel Samad/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jewel Samad/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   One of America's most prominent political dynasties has waded into the growing fight against President Trump's proposed arch in Washington, D.C.   Nine members of the Kennedy family filed suit in federal court on Tuesday to block the 250-foot structure, saying it would obstruct their relatives' gravesites — including the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame — at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.   "A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come," Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said in a statement on behalf of the family.   
   The plaintiffs include children of Sen. Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy and a son of Sen. Edward M. Kennedy, all three of whom are buried at Arlington National Cemetery. There is one noticeable absence: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., did not join his siblings in the lawsuit against his own administration.   "It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in a statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."   Max Kennedy, one of RFK's sons, told NPR's All Things Considered on Wednesday that his family is acting to protect Arlington National Cemetery from "the arbitrary, capricious vanity of one man."   "This is one man who wants to build this arch," he said. "He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved."   The Kennedys' motion, filed hours before Veterans' Day, adds a highly personal layer to the ongoing legal fight.   
   "[The arch] constitutes nothing less than a permanent denigration of the Kennedy Gravesites and the final resting place for Plaintiffs' parents and grandparents," they wrote in their 27-page filing. "Plaintiffs would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended."   The Kennedys seek to join the existing federal lawsuit against the arch, which combines two cases: one brought by Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian earlier this year, and another filed by the governments of D.C. and Virginia late last month. The Arlington County Board has also filed a lawsuit in Virginia.    Loading... 
   The Trump administration has raced its arch through the federal approvals process over the past year, culminating in a final green light from the National Capital Planning Commission on Thursday. Officials had previously said they could break ground in Memorial Circle that same day.   But within moments of the late-night approval, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan stepped in with an order blocking construction for two weeks while she evaluates the broader legal challenges.   
   One of the main arguments against the arch is that its construction is unlawful without congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. The administration maintains that the arch is justified by a century-old authorization of two never-built columns at that same location, which did not seem to convince the judge: Chutkan wrote last week that "merely to state this argument is to reveal its flaws."   The administration has also argued that the case should be thrown out because of plaintiffs' lack of standing, which was the Supreme Court's reasoning in the White House ballroom case. But Chutkan has said D.C. and Virginia likely have standing to sue over the arch, given the financial and logistical harms they would suffer.   
   David Super, a Georgetown University law professor, told NPR in an email that he believes the Kennedys' involvement only strengthens the plaintiffs' standing.   "I can imagine ... that a judge on any level would feel uncomfortable denigrating their concerns over their family graves the way the Supreme Court denigrated the plaintiffs' interest in the White House ballroom case," he wrote. "And coming at a time when the Administration is hinting that it might tear down the Kennedy Center, this certainly makes the President look insensitive or even hostile to his revered predecessor."   Several Kennedy family members have spoken out against Trump's attempted takeover of the Kennedy Center, which is the subject of a separate lawsuit.   Kennedy told NPR that his family acted here in part because they have the unique legal standing to argue the arch will harm them directly. In doing so, he said they can "stand in for the American people because ... this injures everyone in America."   He said his family would have no problem with the arch if it had followed the standard rules and regulations for adding new memorials to D.C., a process that typically includes years of expert and public input.    "All of that has been ignored in this case," Kennedy said. "This arch is being constructed at the whim and whimsy of an autocrat. It's a vanity project, and it's completely different than the memorials that dot the city and that enrich the life of the city."    Arlington National Cemetery is central to the arch fight     
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                JFK's gravesite, featuring an eternal flame, sits just below Arlington House, the former home of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee. Trump's arch would stand in a traffic circle on the bridge that connects Arlington House to D.C.'s National Mall.
                
                    Brendan Smialowksi/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Brendan Smialowksi/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The cemetery says JFK's gravesite is one of its two most-visited locations, along with the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.   The Kennedys explain in their legal filing that JFK's family chose Arlington as his final resting place so that his gravesite could be accessible to the public.   
   "President Kennedy himself visited the Cemetery and stood where he is now buried," they wrote. "The vista looking back toward the District from the spot where his grave now stands was one of his favorites. While looking out, he remarked, 'I could stay here forever.'"   The grave was intentionally placed on the same axis as the bridge connecting Arlington House (the former home of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee) to the Lincoln Memorial, with Kennedy's personal secretary remarking that he was "the link between Lincoln and Lee."   
   Kennedy's gravesite is topped with an eternal flame, which has burned since his funeral in November 1963. The Kennedys said their ancestors were "assured that all aspects of the design would safeguard visibility of the Eternal Flame" from the bridge, even with its intentionally low profile to preserve views of Arlington House.   The arch, they say, would block those views. The Trump administration has acknowledged that the arch would disrupt the historic significance of many nearby memorials, but has said building it anywhere else would defeat its purpose.   The Kennedy complaint goes a step further, citing a recent forensic analysis by the Washington Post that shows the arch would cast shadows over tens of thousands of graves. It would darken JFK's memorial on 50 days of the year, and briefly block the eternal flame on almost half of those.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The Kennedy family members included this photo in their legal filing, showing the eternal flame at JFK's gravesite on the night of his funeral in November 1963.
                
                    Abbie Rowe. White House Photographs. John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, Boston
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Abbie Rowe. White House Photographs. John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, Boston
    

   
   The Trump administration has said the arch will be topped with its own eternal flame, per the controversial lighting recommendations of the Federal Aviation Administration.   The Kennedys said they often visit their family's graves in the morning for extra privacy — exactly the time of day that the Post analysis found the shadows would be most pronounced.   "Plaintiffs' visits to these would literally be shadowed by the Arch, an unlawfully-created structure," the filing reads. "The shadow the Arch would leave over the Kennedy Gravesites would fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the Gravesites."   Arlington National Cemetery is the final resting place for more than 400,000 service members, veterans and their relatives.   
   The White House has characterized the arch as a tribute to the nation's military heritage, saying it will "enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike."   But many of those veterans and their family members have spoken out vehemently against the arch: at protests in Memorial Circle, in tens of thousands of written comments as part of the federal review process, over nearly nine impassioned hours of public testimony during last Thursday's planning commission meeting.   
   Critics say the arch would disrespect those buried at Arlington and disrupt the solemnity of the space for the loved ones who visit them. They say construction — which the Trump administration estimates would involve 20-hour days — would interfere with the 24 to 27 funeral services held there every weekday.   Veterans have said that if Trump — who got five draft deferments during the Vietnam War — really wants to honor their service, he would stop cutting resources for them.   A flurry of court filings argue for a more permanent ban on the arch    The Trump administration has also recast the arch as a military structure (on a public-facing website and in recent court filings), though the plan that received final approval last week has no details about national security. The judge did not seem to find that late-stage argument compelling in her order last week.   In a 10-page declaration filed Tuesday, a retired military general argued that the arch would actually endanger national security.   
   Ret. U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Steven Anderson warned that storing ammunition in a tourist attraction would constitute a "tremendous risk," and that launching drones in that area — especially so close to D.C.'s airport — "poses clear hazards" to civilians.   "Not only is the Arch not suitable for any practical military facility, but it actually degrades security in the National Capital Region by placing a high-payoff target for our enemies just a few meters from a major road network and the traffic circle that surrounds the Arch," Anderson wrote.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Protestors rally beneath a miniature mock-up of the arch during a demonstration at Memorial Circle last Thursday. The administration wants the real version to be 250 feet tall, topped with gold statues and an eternal flame.
                
                    Tom Brenner/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner/Getty Images
    

   
   He pointed to bombings in Beirut in 1983 and Oklahoma in 1995 as "two examples of the danger posed by allowing vehicles within close proximity of comparable military or law enforcement targets."   Anderson's declaration was part of a slew of documents that the veterans filed this week in their quest for a more permanent ban on the arch.   
   Democrats have also vowed to use their forthcoming majority in Congress to block Trump's construction projects and investigate potential wrongdoing.   But experts told NPR earlier this week that given Trump's veto power, Congress is better positioned to tackle that fight through oversight hearings and funding restrictions. The future of the arch, they say, will likely be up to the Supreme Court.

title: Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results
body:
Swing voters Theresa from Pennsylvania, Jason from North Carolina and Gerald from Georgia. All three voted in this year's midterms and all three have mixed emotions about the results.
                
                    Tara Anand for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tara Anand for NPR
    

   
   Republicans were dealt a stunning rebuke in last week's midterms. But swing voters, who could be decisive in the next election, are more interested in results than investigations or impeachment as Democrats prepare to take power in Congress.   "I am hoping that we don't experience a bunch of gridlock and a lot of whining and crying and just political infighting for the next two years," said Theresa, a voter from Pennsylvania who is participating in NPR's Swing Shift project. "I'm hoping we don't have that. I fear that we will have that."   NPR has agreed not to use the full names of the Swing Shift voters, so they can speak freely about politics without fear of personal or professional repercussions.   
    Loading... 
   Theresa voted for President Biden in 2020, President Trump in 2024 and split her ticket in this year's midterms. Like many voters, her top issue this year was affordability. In a voice memo sent to NPR days after the midterms, Theresa said she is eager for the cost of living to come down.   "I just don't remember it ever being as bad in our time," Theresa said. "And I'm just hoping we get some relief and we get some relief soon."   At 9:56 PM on election night, Wally in Georgia hit send on his voice memo. He had seen enough.   "Just checking in here with a quick note. I'm not surprised at all by the outcome tonight," Wally said. "I believe that this is a lot of Trump's doing and pushback on his style of politics and how he governs."   Wally voted for Trump in 2024 but swung back to Democrats in this year's midterms. He had initially supported Trump in hopes that a Trump presidency would shake up the political system, but that didn't happen and now he says the second Trump term has been exhausting. As he sees it, the decisive Democratic wins signal that the country is ready to move on.    
   "Trump has been shooting himself in the foot for many months now," Wally said. "But voting isn't the end of the game here. We have to hold Democrats to some sort of tangible change and not just promises about what they want to do."   For several of the Swing Shift voters, Tuesday's results came as a surprise.   Jason from North Carolina split his ticket, voting for Democrat Roy Cooper for Senate and the Republican incumbent for the House.   "My congressman was defeated this time by someone that no one's really ever heard of," said Jason, sounding almost puzzled by the blue wave that crashed on North Carolina.   That happened in a lot of places. Jason wants the incoming Democratic Congress to focus on the cost of living and steer clear of impeachment.   "My fear is that the Democrats now are going to spend the next 2 years not focusing on any of the things that they say Trump didn't do," said Jason.   Michelle in Michigan, voted for President Biden in 2020 but chose Republicans in 2024 and again in this year's midterms.   "This is the first time I think ever since I've been voting that not one of the people that I voted for won their election," Michelle said.   Michelle says she understands why so many people voted for Democrats, even if she didn't. Americans are tired, she said, of high gas prices, the cost of living and not being able to afford their groceries. They voted for change.   John from Pennsylvania said it felt like his state went from purple to blue overnight.   "I'm just very surprised," John said. "Not surprised that Democrats had a good night, but they had a very good night. Absolutely amazed that they won in Texas and places that just seemed like they were really red."   He voted for President Biden in 2020 and President Trump in 2024. In the most recent midterms, he stuck with Republicans despite concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.   
   Gerald in Georgia ran through the list of states where Democrats won senate races in disbelief.   "Come on man, Texas turned blue," Gerald said. "South Carolina turned blue, Ohio, Kansas. Like, this was a referendum of epic proportions."   Gerald is a Biden to Trump voter from Georgia, who has gone all in on MAGA. He's already looking ahead to a future without Trump leading Republicans.   "The Donald Trump era for all intents and purposes is coming to an end in 2028 for certain, if not before that," Gerald said.   Before that, though, Democrats will take power in Washington, at least in part.   Swing Shift voters said again and again when asked about their hopes and fears following these midterms that they hope that the incoming Democratic Congress will focus on the issues that impact their daily lives but fear more of the same broken politics.   "I will choose to hope because that's really all we can do is hope," said Michelle. "Hope that the politicians that were voted in will live up to the promises they made and that change will truly be made."   Even though John didn't vote for Democrats this year, he still wants them to tackle the cost of living.   "Over these next 2 years I hope they are concerned with and concentrate on the affordability issue," John said. "I hope they work with President Trump to try to lower prices. I just hope it's not two years of investigations and impeachment hearings."   Anything Democrats pass in a divided government would have to be signed by President Trump. The president has been inconsistent in recent days about whether he wants cooperation or combat with the new Congress.

title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race
description: Scott Colom speaks with attendees at an
body:
Scott Colom speaks with attendees at an event held at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson, Miss. on Aug. 1, 2026.
                
                    Sarah Warnock/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Sarah Warnock/AP
    

   
   Democrat Scott Colom has won election to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi, according to a race call by the Associated Press, narrowly defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.   After more than a week of counting outstanding, absentee ballots and affidavit — or provisional — ballots, Colom won the closest Senate race in the country by just a few thousand votes. His victory expands the majority Democrats will have in the new Congress to 55 seats, with the race in Alaska still undecided.    
   In a midterm full of stunning upsets for Democrats, Colom's victory underscores a dramatic shift in the political landscape across the South driven by a surge of Black voter turnout.   Mississippi has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40%, but President Trump won the state by 23 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than 40 years and hasn't sent a Black senator to Washington since Reconstruction.    
   The state's rural, agriculture-heavy economy was disproportionately impacted by rising prices, and saw millions in investment from both parties, particularly in the final weeks of the race. Colom, a district attorney, made cost of living a centerpiece of his campaign message, decrying "Cindy High-Prices" as bad for Mississippi.   Hyde-Smith conceded the race in a video posted to social media shortly after the AP's race call on Wednesday.   "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."   Unlike most other contested Senate races that flipped, Mississippi did not see much national money or attention until the closing days of the election. That included a rally in the final week by President Trump and high-profile visits from former Vice President Kamala Harris, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and other Democrats. The Cook Political Report had the race rated as Likely Republican going into election night.   
   Colom told NPR earlier this month that a lack of investment from national Democrats until the last minute was a mistake.   
   "The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he said. "The Democratic Party has not been trying to win Mississippi. Let's stop kidding ourselves, right? They spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states. They spent almost nothing in Mississippi."   Colom's campaign was a contrast in style from Hyde-Smith, who rarely spoke to reporters in Washington and had minimal presence in the state.   When asked about high beef prices earlier this year, Hyde-Smith — a cattle rancher and onetime state agriculture commissioner — said that "you have so many other proteins to choose from."   That led to a viral campaign ad from Colom, which featured several people expressing disbelief at the senator's suggestion to "pick another protein." Instead, the ad said, it was time to "pick another senator."

title: House effectively ends Hegseth impeachment. And, 3 men accused of plotting U.K. attacks
description: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for
body:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   The House has effectively killed Republican Rep. Thomas Massie's effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The chamber voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment articles back to the House Judiciary Committee for review. The move circumvents any potential floor vote on the impeachment and virtually ensures it won't be addressed before the current Congress session ends. Massie had reintroduced the impeachment articles on Monday, accusing Hegseth of high crimes related to the war with Iran and U.S. strikes against drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon on Nov. 10, 2026.
                
                    Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 NPR's Eric McDaniel describes yesterday's vote to Up First as a game of attendance. There were enough Democrats in Washington to pass the impeachment resolution, but not enough were on the floor to vote, so Republicans had the simple majority. McDaniel spoke to Warren Davidson, a GOP congressman from Ohio, the day before the vote. Davidson said he thinks the war in Iran is unconstitutional, but argued that Hegseth was just a scapegoat for the "status quo politics in Washington."➡️ The GOP had a lot on their agenda yesterday. The Republican-controlled House Oversight Committee released a report on its investigation into the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associates. The report concluded that the federal government mishandled criminal investigations into the disgraced financier and failed survivors.   
   Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio will be the new minority leader of the House. House Republicans voted yesterday to replace Speaker Mike Johnson, who is stepping down after last week's midterm losses. At 62, Jordan brings experience from the House Oversight and Judiciary committees. The two panels are poised to play a central role in the new Congress as Democrats plan investigations into President Trump and his administration.   🎧 NPR's Barbara Sprunt says she viewed the election as a choice between continuity and change, and Jordan clearly represented change. Jordan's selection, along with Stephen Miller's appointment as the president's new chief of staff, highlights a shift towards a combative political approach, Sprunt says. Democratic leadership elections are expected to happen next week and are likely to keep current leaders Hakeem Jeffries in the House and Chuck Schumer in the Senate in place.   U.S. federal prosecutors have indicted three men accused of being Iran-backed operatives allegedly involved in nearly 20 terrorist attacks and attempted attacks in Europe and the U.S. The charges include a plot in September against a British air base where American forces were stationed. The Justice Department says some of these attacks were directed live via FaceTime from Iraq.   
   🎧 Federal prosecutors in Manhattan accuse the men of working for Iran's Revolutionary Guard and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah, both classified as terrorist groups, according to reporter Willem Marx. Seven of the attacks happened in Britain. They included arson, explosives and a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London. Marx also noted that, in a separate case, British counter-terrorism police have arrested a 41-year-old U.S. Army soldier on suspicion of spying for Russia under the National Security Act. Authorities emphasized that this spying investigation is not linked to the Iran-related case. But Marx says these incidents raise significant concerns about security around American military bases in Britain and the safety of nearby residents.Veterans in the new Congress   by Quil Lawrence, Veterans correspondent   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Virginia Democratic Congressional candidate Elaine Luria arrives to deliver remarks during an election night watch party at Holiday Inn Virginia Beach on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Virginia Beach, Virginia. Luria faces incumbent Rep. Jen Kiggans (R-VA) in a rematch after losing to her in Virginia's 2nd District in 2022.
                
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Finn Gomez/Getty Images
    

   
   A Navy admiral fired by the Trump administration is returning to Washington as a Democratic congresswoman. In Virginia, a former Army Colonel beat another former Army Colonel, and a female Navy vet won a rematch to unseat another female Navy vet. In Florida, a staunchly pro-Trump Air Force Vet narrowly fended off a former Army Brigadier General (both also women.) In Montana, two military veterans lost, splitting the votes against a Republican former attorney general with no military background.   What conclusion to draw? There isn't any!   Americans dependably say they admire military service, and political campaigns recruit vets to run on tough races. Whether it works remains an open question, though some research suggests Democrats in particular may benefit from veterans status with voters.   The next Congress includes at least 80 veterans, with a few races still too close to call. And according to With Honor, which supports veteran candidates from both parties who promise to sponsor legislation across the aisle, more than 50 vets in the next Congress have signed their pledge.   But the number of vets is shrinking, down to 15% from the 19% currently in office. That's probably just demographics. Relatively few Americans serve in today's all-volunteer military, while past generations were drafted by the millions to Vietnam and Korea. During World War 2, military service was almost a given for men. When that generation entered politics, both chambers had around 70% veterans for a decade, from 1965 to 1975.   
   The 120th Congress will host more female vets than ever, about double the last class. Analysis by the Veterans Campaign and the University of San Francisco found that Democrats chose veterans as candidates for the toughest races, in districts President Trump won in 2024 by an average of 22 points.   There's another way vets are serving: as poll workers. The group Vet the Vote recruits veterans and their families to help run elections. Starting from a goal of 150,000 volunteers during the 2024 presidential cycle, their campaign counted more than 175,000 for this midterm, from all 50 states, helping bolster the understaffed and overworked polling officials nationwide. The group says it had volunteers in 4 out of 5 zip codes across the country.   And veterans like to vote. Syracuse University D'Aniello Institute for Veterans and Military Families found that vets turned out in relatively higher numbers than civilians in every election since 2014, a difference especially pronounced in midterm elections.   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                In this image, you can see that moment of pause: sometimes the hardest part about talking to other people isn't finding the right words to say, but deciding if you should say anything at all.
                
                    Abi Inman/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Abi Inman/NPR
    

   
   Being honest with people can be tricky. Sometimes, deciding whether to say anything at all can be harder than finding the right words to say. Social psychologist Vanessa Bohns says that giving feedback or criticism often feels like a dilemma. But with care, you can make better choices about when to share your thoughts. Bohns has shared three questions with Life Kit that you could consider before voicing your opinion.   🗣️ Is this information helpful? Honesty is beneficial if your feedback helps someone improve, avoid embarrassment or learn something about themselves. If your comments are mean-spirited, irrelevant or impractical to enact, it's probably better to stay silent.🗣️ Would I want to hear this? Just because you don't want to share the truth doesn't mean the other person doesn't want to hear it. A 2022 survey found that people often underestimate others' desire for feedback even when it is constructive.🗣️ Do they want your feedback? When in doubt, don't assume you know what someone needs. Pre-assessing how valuable your advice is or how well someone can handle the truth can make well-meaning feedback sound patronizing.   
   For more guidance on how to share good and bad news, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                After playing and singing "Little Wonders," by Rob Thomas for Army veteran John Fay at the DC VA Medical Center's Hospice Unit, Musicians On Call performer, Dante Ciolfi, thanks Fay for his service.
                
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
    

   
   Volunteer musicians from Musicians On Call perform for veterans at the VA Medical Center in Washington, D.C., and other hospitalized patients nationwide. They typically visit hospitals three to four times a month.The Rembrandt House Museum in Amsterdam came alive recently as a renowned tattoo artist brought 17th-century masterpieces to life on visitors' skin.The Professional Women's Hockey League has announced the name of its new women's hockey team: the San José Sea Lions. (via KQED)   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: What's behind democratic socialists' historic victories in the midterms?
description:
